templates.pattern: A black hole has a mass of [M] × 10³⁰ kg. Calculate the Schwarzschild radius of the black hole in metres. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
templates.explanation:
Schwarzschild radius Rs = 2GM ÷ c²
= 2 × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × [M] × 10³⁰ ÷ (3 × 10⁸)²
= 2 × 6.67 × [M] × 10¹⁹ ÷ 9 × 10¹⁶
= [RESULT] m

The Schwarzschild radius is the event horizon — the point of no return for a black hole. The Sun's Schwarzschild radius is about 3 km.

templates.pattern: A galaxy has a spectral line at a rest wavelength of [LAM] nm. The observed wavelength is [LAMO] nm. Calculate the redshift z of the galaxy.
templates.explanation:
Redshift z = Δλ ÷ λ
= (λ_observed − λ_rest) ÷ λ_rest
= ([LAMO] − [LAM]) ÷ [LAM]
= [DLAM] ÷ [LAM]
= [RESULT]

Redshift is caused by the expansion of the universe stretching the wavelength of light. A larger redshift means the galaxy is moving away faster and is further away.

templates.pattern: A star has a luminosity of [L] × 10²⁶ W and the flux received at Earth is [F] × 10⁻¹⁰ W/m². Calculate the distance to the star in metres.
templates.explanation:
From F = L ÷ 4πd²:
d = √(L ÷ 4πF)
= √([L] × 10²⁶ ÷ (4π × [F] × 10⁻¹⁰))
= [RESULT] m

This is the standard candle method of measuring distances. If we know the true luminosity and measure the flux we can calculate the distance.

templates.pattern: Planet A orbits a star with period [T1] years and planet B orbits the same star with period [T2] years. Calculate the ratio of their orbital radii r_A ÷ r_B using Kepler's Third Law.
templates.explanation:
Kepler's Third Law: T² ∝ r³
r_A ÷ r_B = (T_A ÷ T_B)^(2/3)
= ([T1] ÷ [T2])^0.667
= [RESULT]

This allows us to find orbital radii from period measurements alone. It applies to all objects orbiting the same central body.

templates.pattern: A satellite of mass [m] kg orbits a planet of mass [M] × 10²⁴ kg at a radius of [R] × 10⁷ m. Calculate the gravitational potential energy of the satellite in joules. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²)
templates.explanation:
Gravitational PE = −GMm ÷ r
= −6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × [M] × 10²⁴ × [m] ÷ ([R] × 10⁷)
= [RESULT] J

Gravitational potential energy is always negative — energy must be supplied to move an object further from the planet. Zero PE is defined at infinite distance.

templates.pattern: A satellite of mass [m] kg orbits a planet of mass [M] × 10²⁴ kg at a radius of [R] × 10⁷ m. Calculate the total orbital energy of the satellite in joules. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²)
templates.explanation:
Total orbital energy E = −GMm ÷ 2r
= −6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × [M] × 10²⁴ × [m] ÷ (2 × [R] × 10⁷)
= [RESULT] J

Total energy = KE + GPE = −GMm/2r. It is always negative for a bound orbit. A satellite in a higher orbit has greater total energy — less negative — but less kinetic energy.

templates.pattern: Star A has luminosity [L1] times the Sun's luminosity and temperature [T1] × 10³ K. Star B has luminosity [L2] times the Sun's luminosity and temperature [T2] × 10³ K. Calculate the ratio of their radii r_A ÷ r_B.
templates.explanation:
From L = 4πr²σT⁴:
r_A ÷ r_B = √(L_A/L_B) × (T_B/T_A)²
= √([L1]/[L2]) × ([T2]/[T1])²
= [RESULT]

This ratio is used to compare the sizes of stars. Red giants are cool but large. Main sequence stars follow a clear pattern on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.

templates.pattern: A planet of mass [m] × 10²⁴ kg orbits a star of mass [M] × 10³⁰ kg at a radius of [R] × 10¹¹ m. Calculate the orbital period of the planet in seconds. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²)
templates.explanation:
From Kepler's Third Law: T² = 4π²r³ ÷ GM
T = √(4π²r³ ÷ GM)
= √(4 × 9.87 × ([R] × 10¹¹)³ ÷ (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × [M] × 10³⁰))
= [RESULT] s

This derivation combines Newton's law of gravitation with circular motion. It allows us to calculate orbital periods from known masses and distances.

templates.pattern: The Hubble constant is [H0] km/s/Mpc. Calculate the critical density of the universe in kg/m³. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg², 1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m)
templates.explanation:
Critical density ρ_c = 3H₀² ÷ 8πG
First convert H₀: [H0] km/s/Mpc = [H0] × 10³ ÷ (3.09 × 10²²) s⁻¹
ρ_c = 3H₀² ÷ (8π × 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)
= [RESULT] kg/m³

The critical density determines the geometry of the universe. If the actual density equals the critical density the universe is flat. The critical density is about 9 × 10⁻²⁷ kg/m³ — extremely sparse.

templates.pattern: A star has a surface temperature of [T] × 10³ K and a radius of [R] × 10⁸ m. Calculate the surface temperature of a second star that has the same luminosity but a radius of [R2] × 10⁸ m in kelvin. (σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²K⁴)
templates.explanation:
Equal luminosity: 4πR²σT⁴ = 4πR₂²σT₂⁴
T₂ = T₁ × (R₁/R₂)^(1/2)
= [T] × 10³ × ([R]/[R2])^0.5
= [RESULT] K

Two stars can have the same luminosity with different combinations of radius and temperature. A larger star can be cooler and still match a smaller hotter star in total power output.
